periods.activity_title: Into the Tunnel: First Reading and Pre-reading Activation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.140): pre-reading personality quiz — paired discussion on adventure types.
Let us discuss — Section I (p.144): train description, tunnel interior, watchman's system.

time_bands.activity: Invite students to share which adventure they would choose from the pre-reading personality options — Bold Explorer, Imaginative Dreamer, Energetic Planner, or Thoughtful Creator. Brief paired exchange, then open to the class for a quick show of hands.

Read Part I of the story aloud, teacher leading with students following in their textbooks (p.140–144). Pause at the train's approach to invite students to describe the sounds and sights in their own words before continuing.

Work through the 'Let us discuss — Section I' questions (p.144) as a whole-class comprehension discussion: how Suraj sensed the train, what he saw inside the tunnel, and the watchman's daily inspection routine. Students respond orally; teacher scribes key phrases on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: The pre-reading quiz is a warm activator, not an assessment — keep the paired exchange quick and conversational so the reading itself gets the bulk of the time. Suraj's description of the train as a magical creature is the richest moment in Part I; linger there and invite students to find the exact phrases Bond uses before moving to the comprehension questions.

periods.activity_title: Night in the Tunnel: Reading Part II and Close Discussion

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss — Section II (p.149): leopard in tunnel, Suraj's fear, the night mail rescue.
Let us think and reflect — Section I (p.149–150): extract questions on darkness, courage, Sunder Singh's axe.

homework.task_brief: Let us think and reflect — Section II (p.150–151): reflective questions on friendship, Sunder Singh as firefly — attempt in writing.

time_bands.activity: Read Part II aloud as a class (p.144–148), with teacher taking the narrator's voice and students reading Sunder Singh's and Suraj's dialogue. Pause before the leopard-in-tunnel scene to ask: what forest sounds have they been hearing, and what do they suggest?

Discuss the 'Let us discuss — Section II' questions (p.149): why Sunder Singh knew the leopard was inside, why Suraj was initially silent, and what finally drove the leopard out. Students answer in pairs first, then share with the class.

Move to the first extract-analysis block (p.149–150): students work on the true/false item about Suraj looking back at the tunnel opening, the MCQ on why he did not stop, and the short-answer on what 'the cutting belonged to the jungle again' means. Teacher takes brief responses from volunteers and clarifies.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the story's night sequence aloud, students are primed to feel the tension of the leopard episode; capitalise on that atmosphere when discussing Suraj's silence and dry throat. A common misreading is that Sunder Singh takes the axe because he is violent — the text supports 'cautious', and it is worth drawing out that distinction explicitly.

periods.activity_title: Directions in Motion: Museum Audio Guide and Trekking Map Conversation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.176): museum treasure-hunt audio guide — mark route on map while listening.
Let us speak (p.144 area): paired role-play — Anju and tour manager giving trekking-site directions.

time_bands.activity: Brief orientation: tell students they will listen to an audio guide for a museum treasure hunt and must track a route on the map provided. Distribute the textbook map (p.176 area) and ask students to locate the entrance hall before the recording begins.

Read the museum audio guide transcript aloud at a measured pace, pausing at each directional instruction so students can mark their maps. Play the recording a second time straight through, after which students compare their routes with a partner and resolve any differences.

Introduce the speaking task: Anju calls the tour manager for directions to the trekking site. Students work in pairs — one as Anju marking the route, one as the tour manager reading the map. Pairs rotate roles once. Teacher circulates, prompting use of the direction phrases from the textbook box.

periods.teacher_notes: The listening and speaking tasks share a direction-giving thread, which makes the transition natural — students who have just marked a museum map are already thinking in spatial terms when the trekking map conversation begins. Watch for students who rush the speaking task; encourage them to pause and confirm understanding at each turn, as Anju would genuinely need to.
materials: Textbook — Let us listen and Let us speak sections (p.176 and speaking page)
Museum and trekking-site maps (textbook or printed copies)
Board and chalk/marker for direction-phrase list

periods.activity_title: The Journey in Words: Descriptive Train-Journey Paragraph

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (writing page): guided descriptive paragraph on a personal train journey — draft and peer response.

time_bands.activity: Teacher models a brief opening sentence for the train-journey paragraph, thinking aloud about sensory detail — sounds of the whistle, the lurch as the train moves. Ask two or three students to contribute a sound, a sight, and a feeling to build a class bank of images on the board.

Walk through the four writing guidelines from 'Let us write' together: boarding impressions, sounds, changing sights, and personal feelings. Students annotate these in their textbook before writing, so the structure is clear.

Students write their descriptive paragraph independently, using the board's image bank and the four guidelines as scaffolding. Teacher circulates, prompting with questions: what could you smell? what did the other passengers do?

Paired peer response: each student reads their partner's paragraph and identifies one strong sensory image and one place where more detail would help. Brief whole-class share of two or three standout images. Students revise within the remaining time.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read Bond's richly sensory account of the train in the story, students have a strong model to draw on — refer them back to the prose if they feel stuck, asking what Bond noticed that they might recreate from their own experience. The commonest weakness at this stage is a list of events rather than a sustained sensory description; the peer-response prompt about a strong image is designed to redirect toward that quality.
materials: Board and chalk/marker for shared image bank
Students' exercise books or writing sheets

periods.activity_title: Sounds of the Tunnel: Vocabulary, Sound Words, and 'Would'

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.151): fill in sentences using tunnel-related phrases — drifting smoke, approaching engine, sawing sound, flickering lights.
Let us learn (p.151–152): match sound words to meanings; complete sentences with correct sound-word forms.
Let us learn (p.152–153): 'would' for habitual past — MCQ on usage, then fill-in using 'used to' or 'would'.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn (p.153): punctuate the Charminar paragraph using brackets, semicolons, and colons.

time_bands.activity: Open with the phrase-completion task (p.151): students predict which of the four box phrases fits each sentence before checking. Briefly elicit why each phrase fits — what picture does 'drifting smoke' create compared with 'approaching engine'?

Introduce the sound-words matching task (p.151): students first guess meanings from memory or context, then verify with a dictionary. Follow with the sentence-completion task (p.152) using the correct form of each sound word; pairs compare answers before a brief class check.

Focus on 'would' for habitual past (p.152–153): teacher reads the watchman's routine sentence aloud and asks why 'would' fits. Students complete the MCQ, then work through the 'used to' / 'would' fill-in passage individually. Class shares answers and the teacher clarifies the distinction between 'used to' (action no longer done) and 'would' (repeated past habit).

periods.teacher_notes: The sound-word set — creaking, chatter, hissing, rustle, puffing — is directly drawn from the story's jungle and railway atmosphere; encourage students to recall where they met each word in the text before consulting the dictionary, as context-first prediction is the stronger vocabulary habit. When teaching 'would' versus 'used to', the commonest confusion is using 'would' with stative verbs (states, not actions); the passage on p.153 contains a stative item ('used to be') that makes this visible naturally.

periods.activity_title: Tunnels and Tracks: Exploring Indian Engineering and Railway History

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (beyond-text page): research Atal Tunnel and Indian Railways history — group presentation of findings.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the Atal Tunnel context from 'Let us explore': world's longest highway tunnel above 10,000 feet, running under Rohtang Pass. Ask students what engineering challenges they imagine building such a tunnel would involve — brief open discussion to activate curiosity.

In groups of four, students use the textbook information plus any available reference material to gather two or three facts each about: the Atal Tunnel's geography and engineering significance, and the history of Indian Railways from the 1853 first journey to today. Each group divides the two topics between members.

Groups present their findings in two minutes each — one student on the tunnel, one on railways. The class notes one new fact they learned from each group. Teacher connects findings back to the story: Sunder Singh's tunnel and Suraj's night-mail ride are part of a 165-year railway story.

Closing reflection: invite students to share, in a sentence each, what they find most remarkable about either the Atal Tunnel or the history of Indian Railways. Teacher summarises the interdisciplinary thread — geography, engineering, history, and literature all meet at the railway tunnel.

periods.teacher_notes: The 'Let us explore' text provides the factual anchors for this unit; students do not need external internet access if the textbook information is treated as the primary source, supplemented by any classroom encyclopaedia or reference book available. A common tendency is for group presentations to become a reading-aloud of facts rather than a discussion of significance — prompt groups to state why their fact is interesting, not just what it is.
materials: Reference books or encyclopaedias if available
Board and chalk/marker for recording class notes

periods.activity_title: The Whole Story: Character, Courage, and the Chapter in Conversation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect — Section II (p.150–151): analytical discussion on Sunder Singh as firefly, the unlikely friendship, jungle philosophy.

time_bands.activity: Open with the story's closing image: Suraj on the night mail, glimpsing Sunder Singh's distant lamp. Ask students — what does this image gather together? Draw out the themes of curiosity, courage, friendship, and the jungle world from the class, noting responses on the board.

Facilitate an analytical discussion around the 'Let us think and reflect — Section II' questions (p.150–151): what Sunder Singh means by lending the tunnel to the Government, his forest-is-safer philosophy, why he is described as a 'firefly', and what draws him and Suraj together despite their age difference. Students build on one another's responses rather than answering in isolation.

Students write a short appreciation (eight to ten sentences) responding to this prompt: Bond's story says that two people in the dark can do a brave, small thing together — write about what the tunnel experience reveals about Suraj and Sunder Singh as a pair. Students complete the piece within the remaining time; a few volunteers share a sentence or two before the unit closes.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws together the story's ideas — the watchman's proprietary love of the tunnel, Suraj's curiosity-driven courage, the jungle's sounds and its leopard — as themes to be analysed rather than plot points to be recalled. The short appreciation is designed to begin and close within these minutes; keep the discussion focused so students have a genuine stretch of uninterrupted writing time.
materials: Textbook — The Tunnel (p.140–151), Let us think and reflect section
Board and chalk/marker for theme notes
Students' exercise books or writing sheets

items.source_lo: Student reads and analyses a prose narrative, retrieving explicit details and making inferences about character, theme, and authorial intent.
items.source_context: Suraj's curiosity, Sunder Singh's tunnel philosophy, leopard rescue, jungle atmosphere, unlikely friendship.
items.item_stem: When Suraj walks through the tunnel alone for the first time, which of the following best describes why he does not stop anywhere inside it?

options.label: A
options.text: The tunnel was flooded with smoke and too dark to see anything worth pausing for.

options.label: B
options.text: He was afraid of being trapped if a train came while he was still inside.

options.label: C
options.text: The dampness and stickiness of the tunnel walls made it unpleasant to linger.

options.label: D
options.text: He was driven by curiosity to reach the other end and see what lay beyond.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Suggests the student is confusing the sensory atmosphere of the tunnel with Suraj's reason for moving — Bond describes smoke and darkness but Suraj's motivation is curiosity, not obstruction.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Conflates the danger of the night-mail episode (Part II) with Suraj's solo daytime walk — the train schedule is not the driver here.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Picks up on the textual detail that the tunnel is damp and sticky but misreads it as a reason to hurry rather than a sensory observation Bond makes in passing.

items.source_lo: Student reads and analyses a prose narrative, retrieving explicit details and making inferences about character, theme, and authorial intent.
items.source_context: Suraj's curiosity, Sunder Singh's tunnel philosophy, leopard rescue, jungle atmosphere, unlikely friendship.
items.item_stem: Sunder Singh tells Suraj that he has 'lent his tunnel to the Government'. Analyse what this remark reveals about Sunder Singh's relationship with the tunnel and his sense of identity. Support your answer with at least two details from the story.

expected_elements: Identifies Sunder Singh's proprietary sense of belonging to the tunnel and jungle.
Notes his pride in caring for the tunnel despite its official ownership.
Links this attitude to his broader jungle philosophy — forest as home, not workplace.
Supports with at least one specific detail from the prose (inspection routine, leopard knowledge, or lamp).

items.source_context: Museum treasure-hunt audio guide: entrance hall, art gallery, weapons room, musical instruments section, auditorium.
items.item_stem: A group of students listened to the museum audio guide during the treasure hunt. Based on the route described in the guide, which room did they reach immediately after leaving the Art Gallery through the third door on the right?

what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses the third door with the first door on the left, which leads to the Decorative Art Gallery — a sequencing error in following the directions.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Jumps ahead to the final destination without tracking the intermediate rooms — the auditorium is reached from the Musical Instruments Section, not directly from the Art Gallery.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Mistakes the Musical Instruments Section for the immediate next room; that section follows a left turn from the Weapons Room, not a direct exit from the Art Gallery.

items.item_stem: The museum audio guide describes a route from the Entrance Hall to where the treasure is hidden. Fill in the blanks to complete the route: Start at the Entrance Hall → walk straight to reach the (1) __________ → exit through the third door on the right into the (2) __________ → take a left turn to find the (3) __________ → enter the second room to the left to reach the (4) __________, where the treasure is hidden.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. Art Gallery; 2. Weapons Room; 3. Musical Instruments Section; 4. Auditorium.

items.item_stem: You are Anju, calling the tour manager to ask for directions from the railway station to the trekking site. Describe clearly the route you are told to follow, using at least four direction phrases (such as turn left, keep going straight, take the next right, in front of). Your partner will play the tour manager and give the directions from the map.

expected_elements: Uses at least four direction phrases correctly and in sequence.
Confirms understanding at each turn with a follow-up question or repetition.
Maintains appropriate telephone register — polite and clear.
Marks the route accurately on the map as directions are received.

items.item_stem: Imagine you are the tour manager and Anju has just arrived at the wrong location because she misunderstood one of your directions. Role-play a brief telephone conversation in which you identify where the misunderstanding happened, politely correct it, and give revised directions to get her back on track. Give a reason for why you think the confusion occurred.

expected_elements: Identifies the specific direction that caused the confusion.
Gives a revised, clear directional sequence using spatial phrases.
Maintains a polite and helpful tone appropriate to the role.
Offers a plausible reason for the misunderstanding (e.g., ambiguous landmark, missing turn instruction).

items.source_lo: Student plans and drafts a descriptive paragraph, integrating sensory detail, personal experience, and structured narrative progression.
items.source_context: Personal train journey: boarding impressions, sounds of whistle and wheels, changing scenery, feelings of excitement or curiosity.
items.item_stem: Write a descriptive paragraph about the moment a train you were travelling on pulled out of a station. Use the following prompts to structure your paragraph: (i) What you saw and heard as the train began to move. (ii) How the scenery changed as the station disappeared behind you. (iii) One feeling you had as the journey began. Your paragraph should be six to eight sentences long and use at least two specific sensory details.

expected_elements: Describes the departure moment with at least two sensory details (sound, sight, or feeling).
Shows a clear progression from the station to the open journey.
Includes a personal feeling or emotional response to the journey.
Maintains descriptive rather than narrative-list structure throughout.

items.source_lo: Student plans and drafts a descriptive paragraph, integrating sensory detail, personal experience, and structured narrative progression.
items.source_context: Personal train journey: boarding impressions, sounds of whistle and wheels, changing scenery, feelings of excitement or curiosity.
items.item_stem: In 'The Tunnel', Ruskin Bond uses the night mail train as a symbol of connection — it links Suraj to Sunder Singh even after they part. Write a short composition (two paragraphs) imagining you are on a long overnight train journey for the first time. In your first paragraph, describe the atmosphere inside the train as night falls. In your second paragraph, reflect on what a journey through darkness makes you think or feel — about the places you are leaving, the unknown ahead, or the people around you. Write freely and imaginatively; there is no single correct response.

expected_elements: First paragraph sustains an atmospheric, sensory description of the night train interior.
Second paragraph moves to personal reflection — not a list of facts but genuine feeling.
Writing shows imaginative engagement rather than repetition of story plot.
Both paragraphs use varied sentence structures and specific, concrete detail.

items.source_context: Sound words (creaking, hissing, rustle, puffing, chatter); tunnel-atmosphere phrases; 'would' and 'used to' for past habits.
items.item_stem: Match each sound word from the story with the description of what it conveys.
items.visual_stimulus:
Sound Word | What it conveys
creaking | the long, low groan of a wooden beam or door as it moves
puffing | short, quick blasts of air or steam, as from an engine
rustle | a soft, dry sound made by leaves or paper moving gently
hissing | a drawn-out 's' sound, like steam escaping or a snake's warning
chatter | a rapid series of short, high sounds made by birds or monkeys

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: creaking – the long, low groan of a wooden beam or door as it moves; puffing – short, quick blasts of air or steam, as from an engine; rustle – a soft, dry sound made by leaves or paper moving gently; hissing – a drawn-out 's' sound, like steam escaping or a snake's warning; chatter – a rapid series of short, high sounds made by birds or monkeys.

answer_key.right: the long, low groan of a wooden beam or door as it moves
short, quick blasts of air or steam, as from an engine
a soft, dry sound made by leaves or paper moving gently
a drawn-out 's' sound, like steam escaping or a snake's warning
a rapid series of short, high sounds made by birds or monkeys

items.source_context: Sound words (creaking, hissing, rustle, puffing, chatter); tunnel-atmosphere phrases; 'would' and 'used to' for past habits.
items.item_stem:
Sunder Singh was the watchman of the tunnel for many years. Read the sentences below about his routine and his life, and fill in each blank with 'used to' or 'would'. More than one answer may be correct for some blanks — write the one that fits the sentence best and be ready to explain why.

(1) Every evening, Sunder Singh __________ light his lamp before stepping into the tunnel.
(2) He __________ live in a small hut beside the railway cutting — but he does not live there any more.
(3) Whenever a train approached, he __________ walk the length of the tunnel to check for danger.
(4) In those years, the jungle __________ feel alive with the calls of deer and nightjars after dark.
(5) He __________ keep an axe leaning against the wall of his hut, always within reach.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. would; 2. used to (signals the action no longer occurs — 'used to' is the better fit here); 3. would; 4. used to / would (stative verbs like 'feel' prefer 'used to'; accept 'would' if student justifies it as a repeated experience); 5. would.

items.source_lo: Student connects a literary text to real-world engineering and historical contexts through interdisciplinary research and oral presentation.
items.source_context: Atal Tunnel under Rohtang Pass; Indian Railways history from 1853 first journey to present day.
items.item_stem: The textbook's 'Let us explore' section tells us that the Atal Tunnel is 9.02 kilometres long and runs under the Rohtang Pass, and that India's first passenger train ran on 16 April 1853. Using these two facts as your starting points, write an extended response that: (i) explains why a tunnel through a mountain pass like Rohtang would be considered an engineering achievement, and (ii) describes what you think travelling by train in 1853 might have felt like compared with train travel today.

expected_elements: Explains at least one specific engineering challenge of building under a high mountain pass.
Uses the 9.02 km length or the 10,000-feet altitude as evidence of the achievement.
Draws a reasoned contrast between 1853 rail travel and travel today.
Connects the interdisciplinary content back to the story's railway world.

items.source_lo: Student connects a literary text to real-world engineering and historical contexts through interdisciplinary research and oral presentation.
items.source_context: Atal Tunnel under Rohtang Pass; Indian Railways history from 1853 first journey to present day.
items.item_stem: Design a short research project titled 'Tunnels and Tracks: India's Engineering Stories'. Your project should: (i) identify TWO tunnels or railway routes in India (including the Atal Tunnel) that are remarkable for their location, length, or history; (ii) explain what geographical challenge each one overcomes; and (iii) include a reflection on how Ruskin Bond's fictional tunnel in 'The Tunnel' connects to the real story of Indian railway engineering. Present your findings as a structured report or illustrated poster with at least three clearly labelled sections.

expected_elements: Identifies two specific Indian tunnels or railway routes with accurate factual detail.
Explains the geographical challenge each route or tunnel addresses.
Connects Bond's fictional tunnel to the broader railway engineering narrative.
Presents findings in a structured format with clearly labelled sections.
